chunks: "Daisy-chaining means connecting SPI slaves in series so they act like one long shift register.
The master's MOSI goes into slave 1's data input, slave 1's data output goes into slave 2's input, and so on, and the last slave's output returns to the master's MISO.
SCLK and chip select are shared by all of them, so it's four wires no matter how many devices.
To use it, I pull CS low and clock out enough bits to fill every device: with N devices of 16 bits each that's 16N clocks.
Data flows down the chain as it shifts, so the first word I send ends up in the last device, and the last word I send stays in the first.
When I raise CS, each device latches whatever is in its shift register, so all of them update at the same time.
While I'm sending, whatever was in the chain comes back on MISO, which is how I read results. The advantages are the minimal wiring and simultaneous updates.

The disadvantages are that every transaction has to move data for the whole chain, even to change one device; latency grows with chain length; and only parts that support it, with a data output and latch-on-CS behaviour, can be chained.
Common examples are 74HC595 shift registers, LED drivers, DAC and ADC arrays."
